title: Cross-payment does not actually cancel anyone’s debt until applied by faith and repentance
source_text: XIX. At, inquies, antequam Electus aliquis credat & convertatur, Christus jam in cruce persolvit poenas peccatis illius debitas: ac proinde illarum amplius debitor non est apud Dei tribunal: nec enim amplius quis tenetur debito quod vas ejus pro illo exsolvit. Qui autem non est amplius apud Deum debitor poenae, quam peccata ejus alioqui merentur, annon actu illi peccata remissa sunt? Respondeo quod Christus pro nobis in cruce praestitit illud est, ut mediante fide atque poenitentia, possimus a Deo veniam peccatorum consequi, non obstante amplius justitia divina, cui per mortem Christi satisfactum est. Sed mortis Christi pretium nullius debitum & reatum actu tollit, nisi prius ipsi applicetur per fidem & poenitentiam. Adeoque in morte Christi habemus quidem pretium sufficiens quod pro peccatis nostris Deo offerre possimus, sed eorum nomine & reatu poenae semper rei tenemur, donec pretium illud fide amplexi nostrum fecerimus, ac tale factum Deo obtulerimus. Itaque Christi morte & passione remissio peccatorum nobis quidem impetrata est, sub conditione fidei, quae comitem habet poenitentiam & resipiscentiam: sed remissio peccatorum nobis actu concessa minime censeri debet, priusquam conditionem illam impleverimus, & mors Christi nobis fuerit per fidem applicata.
pass_a_gloss: But, you will say: before any elect person believes and is converted, Christ has already on the cross paid the penalties owed for that person’s sins; and therefore he is no longer a debtor for them before God’s tribunal—for no one is any longer held to a debt which his surety has paid for him. But he who is no longer a debtor before God for the penalty which his sins otherwise deserve—have sins not actually been remitted to him? I answer: what Christ rendered for us on the cross is this, that by the mediation of faith and repentance we may be able to obtain from God pardon of sins, divine justice no longer standing in the way, to which satisfaction has been made through Christ’s death. But the price of Christ’s death actually takes away no one’s debt and guilt unless it is first applied to him through faith and repentance. And so in Christ’s death we indeed have a sufficient price which we can offer to God for our sins, but in their name and by the guilt of penalty we always remain liable until, having embraced that price by faith, we have made it ours and offered it so made to God. Therefore by Christ’s death and passion remission of sins has indeed been obtained for us under the condition of faith, which has repentance and amendment as companion; but remission of sins ought by no means to be reckoned as actually granted to us before we have fulfilled that condition and Christ’s death has been applied to us through faith.
pass_b_english: Surety-payment on the cross opens a mediated path; it does not automatically clear each person’s debt.
Sufficient price is ours only when faith-and-repentance apply it—until then liability remains.
